ex_en: The house is on this street.
The road is jammed today.
I go to the mosque to pray the Friday prayer.
note: pl. جوامع jwāmi3. جامع is the everyday word; مسجد is more formal.

ex_en: I went to the bank to withdraw money.
note: pl. مصارف maSārif. Libyan banks are officially called مصرف; بنك bank is also understood.

ex_en: The post office is closed today.
Call the police now!
We went to the police station to report it.
Martyrs' Square is in the center of Tripoli.
I live in Tripoli.
note: Capital of Libya. Locals pronounce it Trābles (also Trāblus).

ex_en: My brother works in Benghazi.
note: Libya's second city, capital of the east (Barga).

ex_en: Misrata is famous for trade.
Sabha is in the south.
note: Main city of the Fezzan region.

ex_en: Zawiya is close to Tripoli.
The people of the neighborhood all know me.
note: pl. حوم 7wam. Very Libyan/Maghrebi; ولد حومة = a local guy from the area.

ex_en: The old city is very beautiful.
note: pl. مدن mudun. المدينة القديمة = Tripoli's old walled medina.

ex_en: My grandfather lives in a small village.
We live in a new apartment building.
Go over the bridge.
note: From Turkish köprü. pl. كباري kbāri. جسر jisr is also used.

ex_en: Stop at the traffic light.
Turn right at the roundabout.
note: Roundabouts are key landmarks when giving directions in Libyan cities.

ex_en: We stroll along the corniche at night.
You have to go to the municipality to get the document.
I have to go to the embassy to get a visa.
I'll fill up with petrol at the station.
note: On its own it usually means a petrol station.

ex_ar: الحوش في الزنقة اللي ورا الجامع.
ex_en: The house is in the alley behind the mosque.
Let's go downtown to shop.
note: Libyans often say just البلاد il-blād for "town center".

ex_en: The kids are playing in the park.

ex_ar: امشي على الرصيف مش في الطريق.
ex_en: Walk on the sidewalk, not in the road.
This building has ten floors.
I go to the club every day.
note: pl. نوادي nawādi. Tripoli clubs Al-Ahly and Al-Ittihad are football rivals.

ex_en: The cemetery is behind the mosque.
The airport is near Souq al-Juma.
note: Large district of eastern Tripoli; Mitiga airport is there.

ex_en: The Green Mountain is cold in winter.
note: Forested highland region in eastern Libya, around al-Bayda.

ex_en: My car is at the mechanic's.
note: From Italian macchina. pl. مكاين mkāyin. Very common Libyan word for car.

ex_en: I bought a new car.
note: pl. سيارات. More formal than مكينة makīna but widely used.

ex_en: In the old days people rode in horse carriages.
Take a taxi to the airport.
The bus stops in front of the school.
The plane takes off at nine o'clock.
I'll drive you to the airport.
Don't forget your passport!
note: Short for جواز سفر jawāz safar.

ex_en: I booked a ticket to Tunis.

ex_ar: نزلنا في فندق قريب من البحر.
ex_tr: nzilna fi fundug grīb min il-ba7ar.
ex_en: We stayed at a hotel near the sea.
How was the trip?
I love travelling a lot.
The flight was delayed two hours.
note: pl. رحلات. Also used for school or family outings.

ex_en: The suitcase is very heavy.
Turn to the right.
The bank is on the left.
Show me the map on the phone.
The visa takes a month.
The ship arrived at the port.
We travelled by ship to Malta.
note: From Italian vapore "steam(er)". pl. بوابير bwābīr

ex_en: The fishermen went out in the boat.
note: From Italian feluca. pl. فلايك flāyik

ex_en: My brother rides a motorbike.
The little one wants a bicycle.
note: From Italian bicicletta via Maghrebi usage.

ex_en: Petrol is cheap in Libya.
I got my driving license last month.
The tire is flat.
Slowly, there's a speed bump.
We were stuck in traffic for an hour.
The driver took us home.
The passengers are waiting at the airport.
note: Also adj "travelling, away": هو مسافر = he's away.

ex_en: I have a reservation at the hotel.
They searched the suitcase at customs.
The border with Tunisia is crowded.
note: Ras Ajdir (راس جدير) is the main crossing to Tunisia.

ex_en: Benghazi is in the east.
Tripoli is in the west.
The sea is to the north.
The desert is in the south.
What is your address?
We're going to the sea on Friday.
note: pl. بحور b7ūr. Libyans say "the sea" for going to the beach.

ex_en: The beach is full of people in summer.
The Libyan desert is huge.
The sand is hot at midday.
note: القايلة il-gāyla = the hot midday hours.

ex_en: We went up to the mountain in spring.
note: pl. جبال jbāl. الجبل often means the Nafusa Mountains (جبل نفوسة) in the west.

ex_en: Sit under the tree in the shade.
The sun is scorching today.
The moon is full tonight.
note: Libyan/Maghrebi feminine form; قمر gamar also heard.

ex_en: The sky is full of stars.
The sky is clear today.
Rain is scarce in Libya.
note: See also شتا shta, the everyday Libyan word for rain.

ex_en: It's pouring rain outside!
The wind is strong today.
The weather is nice today.
The heat is unbearable in August.
The cold at night is biting.
The ghibli came and everything is dusty.
note: Hot, dry, dusty southerly wind; lit. "from the qibla/south". English "ghibli" comes from this.

en: dust storm; dust in the air
ex_en: Close the window, there's dust blowing.

ex_ar: في الصيف نمشوا للبحر كل يوم.
ex_en: In summer we go to the sea every day.
Autumn in Libya is short.
Spring is the nicest season.
What's your favorite season?
note: pl. فصول fSūl. Also "classroom" in school context.

ex_en: The clouds covered the sun.
Snow fell in the mountains.
There's fog on the road in the morning.
The wadi filled up after the rain.
There's a water spring in the mountain.
The water is from the well.
This palm tree has lots of dates.
My grandfather planted this olive tree.
I brought her a flower.
The grass has grown tall in the garden.
There's a big rock in the road.
The kids are playing in the dirt.
The sea is wavy today.
Djerba is an island in Tunisia.
Ghadames is an oasis in the desert.
There's a forest in the Green Mountain.
I saw the lightning yesterday.
The thunder scared the kids.
Sit in the shade, the sun is hot.
I love nature and quiet.
The temperature today is forty.
The road passes beside the salt flat.
note: Common landscape feature on the Libyan coast.

ex_en: Do you have a pet at home?
The camel can endure thirst.
note: pl. جمال jmāl. Camel meat is eaten in Libya, especially in the south.

ex_en: She-camel's milk is healthy.
The camel calf walks behind its mother.
This horse runs fast.
note: pl. خيل khēl. Horses are central to Libyan festivals and fantasia shows.

ex_en: This mare is a purebred Arabian.
The farmer rides the donkey.
note: pl. حمير 7mīr. Also a common insult ("idiot").

ex_en: The mule carries the heavy load.
The dog barks at night.
We found a little puppy in the street.
The cat is sleeping on the chair.
note: Libyan word; female قطوسة gaTTūsa. pl. قطاطيس gTāTīs

ex_en: We bought a sheep for Eid.
note: Very Libyan word. pl. علاليش 3lālīsh. The Eid al-Adha sheep is the علوش العيد.

ex_en: This ram has big horns.
The ewe just gave birth.
The shepherd takes the flock out to graze.
The goat eats everything.
The cow gives milk.
The hen laid an egg.
The rooster crows early in the morning.
The birds sing in the garden.
He keeps pigeons on the roof.
note: Collective حمام 7mām. Pigeon keeping is a popular hobby.

ex_en: There's a mouse in the kitchen!
Watch out, there's a snake!
There are lots of scorpions in the south.
There are lots of flies in summer.
The mosquitoes didn't let me sleep.
The ants came to the sugar.
I saw a cockroach in the bathroom.
The tortoise walks very slowly.
note: Maghrebi word (Amazigh origin). pl. فكارين fkārīn

ex_en: The wolf ate the sheep.
note: pl. ذياب dhyāb. In Libya often refers to the golden jackal/African wolf.

ex_en: The gazelle runs fast.
note: pl. غزلان ghizlān. Also a compliment for a beautiful woman.

ex_en: The kids love the rabbit.
The fennec fox lives in the desert.
note: Small desert fox with big ears.

ex_en: Bees make honey.
We saw the lion at the zoo.
note: pl. أسود usūd. Also used as a nickname for a brave man.

ex_en: I'm off to work.
note: The everyday Libyan word for work. pl. خدمات

ex_en: I found a job at an oil company.
The workers started work early in the morning.
My father is a government employee.
note: pl. موظفين mwaDHDHfīn. Most Libyans work in the public sector.

ex_en: The manager is in his office.
The boss didn't come in today.
My son is an engineer at the oil company.
The teacher explained the lesson well.
note: Fem. أستاذة ustādha. Also a respectful title for educated men.

ex_en: The master blacksmith is skilled.
The policeman stopped me at the traffic light.
The salary hasn't been paid this month.
note: Libyan usage; pl. مرتبات murattabāt. "نزل المرتب" = the salary came in.

ex_en: I work at a private company.
We have a meeting at ten.
You need to talk to a lawyer.
The carpenter fixed the door.
The car is at the mechanic's.
His uncle is a merchant in the gold market.
The farmer is planting barley.
The builder is building the house.
Get an electrician to fix the electricity.
I go to the barber every Friday.
Work starts at eight o'clock.
I took a week's leave.
I signed the contract today.
He wants to open a small business.
He worked for years in the factory.
His brother is a soldier.
The journalist questioned the director.
I need your signature here.
The paper needs a stamp.
note: pl. أختام. Libyan bureaucracy runs on stamps.

ex_en: My grandfather lives on his pension.
He's been unemployed for a year.
The kids are at school now.
I study at the University of Tripoli.
He's in the faculty of medicine.
I'm a third-year student.
The pupils came out of school.
School starts in September.
note: Libyan: from قرا gra "to read/study". "يقرا" = he studies.

ex_en: Today's lesson is hard.
I forgot the book at home.
Do you have a pen I can borrow?
Write in the notebook.
I have an exam tomorrow.
Did you finish your homework?
How many languages do you know?
I speak Libyan Arabic.
Do you speak English?
My grandfather knows Italian.
note: Libya was an Italian colony (1911–1943); many Libyan words come from Italian.

ex_en: The teacher wrote on the board.
Bring the ruler and the pen.
The results are out, I passed!
He got his secondary school certificate.
I study in the library.
Open the book to page twenty.
I have a question, teacher.
The answer is wrong.
My son is good at math.
I like history class.
What does this word mean?
Arabic has twenty-eight letters.
Look the word up in the dictionary.
My daughter is in kindergarten.
At break we play football.
My phone is switched off.
Give me your mobile number.
note: Libyan word for cell phone; موبايل mōbāyl also used.

ex_en: The mobile fell and broke.
The internet is down today.
Do you have an iPhone charger?
The phone has no charge.
The battery is dead.
I work on the computer all day.
I brought the laptop with me.
He sent me a message on WhatsApp.
note: pl. رسايل rsāyil. مسج masaj is also used.

ex_en: I have an important call.
Give me a ring (missed call) when you arrive.
Take a picture of us.
Did you see the video I sent?
The phone's camera is good.
I forgot the password.
Download this app.
I don't have any credit.
note: Prepaid phone credit; also bank balance.

ex_en: I bought a Libyana top-up card.
note: Libyana and Al-Madar are the main Libyan mobile networks.

ex_en: I need a new SIM card.
There's no signal here.
The screen cracked.
Put on headphones, it's loud.
The power has been out since morning.
note: Very Libyan: ضو/ضي = electricity. Power cuts (طفي الضي) are a daily topic.

ex_en: Turn on the generator, the power's out.
note: Many Libyan homes have one because of power cuts.

ex_en: Put the files on the flash drive.
The printer is out of ink.
I sent you an email.
Do you have a Facebook account?
note: Facebook is the dominant social network in Libya.

ex_en: The download is very slow.
This show is funny.
Happy Eid!
note: pl. أعياد a3yād. Greeting: عيدكم مبروك / كل عام وانتو بخير.

ex_en: On the Big Eid we slaughter the sheep.
The Small Eid comes after Ramadan.
Ramadan Kareem!
Fasting in summer is hard.
My cousin's wedding is on Thursday.
note: pl. أعراس a3rās. Libyan weddings last several days.

ex_en: The henna night is a day before the wedding.
The wedding singers sang all night.
note: Libyan tradition: women's troupes with drums at weddings. pl. زمزامات

ex_en: It's time for prayer.
Did you hear the call to prayer?
God protect you.
note: Appears in countless everyday phrases: إن شاء الله, الحمد لله, ما شاء الله.

ex_en: Don't forget us in your prayers.
He has memorized the whole Quran.
note: Pronounced with q, as a religious word.

ex_ar: أمي مشت للحج العام اللي فات.
ex_tr: ummi mshat lil-7ajj il-3ām illi fāt.
ex_en: My mother went on Hajj last year.
note: A returning pilgrim is called الحاج il-7ājj / الحاجة il-7ājja.

ex_en: On the Mawlid we eat asida.
note: Widely celebrated in Libya with asida and children's lanterns (قناديل).

ex_en: The kids are waiting for their Eid money.
Do you like Libyan music?
The malouf group sang at the wedding.
note: Traditional urban music of Tripoli, of Andalusian origin.

ex_en: The sound of the zukra is joyful.
note: Traditional bagpipe played at weddings and celebrations.

ex_en: This song is lovely.
We play football in the neighborhood.
The match is tonight at nine.
What's your team, Al-Ahly or Al-Ittihad?
Goal! We won!
The stadium is full of fans.
The Libyan flag is red, black and green.
note: pl. أعلام a3lām. Also the name of a Bedouin poetry genre (غناوة العلم).

ex_en: I love my country.
Libya is in North Africa.
Tomorrow is a public holiday.
We threw a party for his success.
We went to the condolence gathering in the neighborhood.
note: Usually held for three days in a tent or the family home.

ex_en: We have many wedding customs.
note: Singular عادة 3āda; often paired: العادات والتقاليد.

ex_en: Islam is the religion of most Libyans.
This meat is halal.
Give him some charity.
The government paid out the salaries.
In Ramadan we watch TV series.
note: Ramadan is the peak season for series.
